meta.title: Who really said "Blood, sweat and tears"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Churchill made it famous on 13 May 1940 — but he actually said "blood, toil, tears and sweat." The popular three-word form is a condensed misquote of an older phrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Blood, sweat and tears'?
meta.ogDescription: Churchill's real words were "blood, toil, tears and sweat" (13 May 1940). The famous three-word version drops "toil" — and the phrase predates him.

answer.label: Not Churchill’s exact words — a condensed misquote
answer.sourceLine: Churchill made the phrase famous, but on 13 May 1940, in his first speech as Prime Minister, he actually told the House of Commons: “I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat.” The popular three-word “blood, sweat and tears” drops ‘toil’ and reorders the last two words — a condensation the press adopted almost immediately. The phrase itself also predates him, appearing in John Donne, Byron and Theodore Roosevelt.

source.heading: What Churchill actually said

docMeta.dd: First speech as Prime Minister, House of Commons

source.excerpt: I would say to the House, as I said to those who have joined this Government: ‘I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat.’
trail: The International Churchill Society gives the verbatim line as “blood, toil, tears and sweat” — four nouns, with ‘toil’ where the popular version has nothing.
Wikipedia’s article “Blood, toil, tears and sweat” notes the modern “blood, sweat and tears” reorders and simplifies his wording.
Word-historian sources trace the phrase to John Donne (1611), Byron (1823) and Theodore Roosevelt (1897) — well before Churchill.
Churchill scholar Richard Langworth shows Churchill himself used kindred phrasing earlier, e.g. “Their sweat, their tears, their blood” (1931).
source.excerptNote: The familiar three-word “blood, sweat and tears” never appears in the speech — it is a later shortening of this line.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from Churchill’s speech of 13 May 1940, first published that year and therefore still in copyright (Churchill died in 1965). The underlying metaphor is centuries old and long public-domain, but the famous 1940 formulation is a protected work of the Churchill literary estate.

author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, wartime Prime Minister & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill led Britain as Prime Minister (1940–45 and 1951–55) and was one of the 20th century’s most quoted orators. His speeches of 1940 — delivered as France fell and Britain faced invasion — are among the most celebrated in the English language. He was also a prolific author and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

misattribution.heading: How the wording got mangled
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine Churchill line that the public has been quoting wrong for over 80 years — and the underlying phrase was never his to begin with.

items.why: He said “I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat” on 13 May 1940. The popular “blood, sweat and tears” drops ‘toil’ and swaps the order of the last two words — a press-era condensation.
“Blood, sweat and tears” imagery appears in John Donne (1611), Byron’s The Age of Bronze (1823) and Theodore Roosevelt (1897), so Churchill neither coined nor first combined the three words.

misattribution.truthLine: Real speaker, real occasion — wrong words: Churchill said “blood, toil, tears and sweat,” per the International Churchill Society.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Churchill spoke these words three days after becoming Prime Minister, as German forces swept into France and the Low Countries. It was his first address to the Commons as PM — a deliberately unglamorous promise of hardship rather than easy victory, setting the tone for Britain’s war leadership.

The line became one of the most quoted passages in English oratory, which is exactly why its slippage into “blood, sweat and tears” is so telling: the public remembers the rhythm and the spirit, but not the actual fourth word, ‘toil.’
